claims.text: A ferromagnetic ground state can be identified using spin-polarized density functional theory calculations that compare the total energies of different spin configurations.
If the ferromagnetic configuration has lower total energy than the other tested configurations, the material has a ferromagnetic ground state.
The material of interest is a multicomponent alloy of 3d transition metals whose magnetic ground state has not been verified.
Ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, and nonmagnetic configurations should be compared using spin-polarized DFT.
Ground-state electronic-structure calculations are typically performed at 0 K.
Standard exchange-correlation functionals can be used for these calculations.
The relevant structural mediator is spin polarization of d-band electrons in the crystal lattice.
Spin-polarized DFT accounts for exchange-correlation interactions involved in the energies of magnetic configurations.
The energetically favored spin arrangement indicates the ground-state magnetic order.
The ferromagnetic configuration is predicted to have a lower total energy than the alternatives.
A lower total energy for the ferromagnetic configuration confirms a stable ferromagnetic ground state.
Paramagnetic, antiferromagnetic, or nonmagnetic configurations of the same material structure provide reference baselines.
The proposed comparison is primarily applicable to zero-temperature or low-temperature theoretical predictions.
Finite-temperature magnetic effects may require additional treatments such as spin-fluctuation methods.
Strong electron correlation or spin-orbit coupling may create complications beyond standard DFT.
Some systems may therefore require more advanced computational approaches.
Low-temperature magnetization measurements can test whether the alloy has spontaneous magnetization.
The proposed measurements are temperature-dependent magnetization, saturation magnetization, and coercivity.
Failure to observe spontaneous magnetization at low temperature would falsify the hypothesis.
